# Fresh food prevents scurvy (citrus, vitamin C) (`scurvy_citrus`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by controlled_trial, vitamins_deficiency
- Core idea: Scurvy (bleeding gums, old wounds reopening, exhaustion, death) appears after six weeks to three months without fresh food and is not catching. The body needs a small daily amount of a substance found in fresh fruit and vegetables and in fresh, lightly cooked meat. The juice of one lemon or orange a day prevents and cures it within a week or two. The substance is destroyed by boiling down, long storage, air and copper vessels, so use fresh juice or juice preserved cold with spirit, sprouted beans or peas, sauerkraut, fresh potatoes, or a tea of fresh pine or spruce needles steeped, not boiled.
- Pitfalls:
  - Preserving the juice by boiling it down to a syrup, which is why Lind's own 'rob' failed
  - Thinking sourness is what cures and substituting vinegar or acid, as navies did
  - Assuming all citrus is equal: West Indian limes hold far less than lemons, and scurvy returned to British ships and polar expeditions after 1860
  - Blaming idleness, damp, salt meat or bad air, or treating it as contagious
  - Saying Lind's trial ended scurvy; the navy took 40 years to act, and Lind himself stayed unsure of the cause
- History: americas: 1536 – St Lawrence Iroquoians cure Cartier's crew with a decoction of a conifer ('annedda', probably white cedar); europe: 1601 – Lancaster gives lemon juice on an East India voyage; 1617 Woodall's Surgions Mate recommends it; 1747 Lind's comparative trial on HMS Salisbury (published 1753); 1795 Royal Navy issues lemon juice; 1907 Holst and Frølich produce scurvy in guinea pigs; 1928–1932 Szent-Györgyi and King isolate vitamin C
- Read:
  - James Lind, A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753)
  - Kenneth J. Carpenter, The History of Scurvy and Vitamin C (1986)
  - Stephen R. Bown, Scurvy: How a Surgeon, a Mariner, and a Gentleman Solved the Greatest Medical Mystery of the Age of Sail (2003)
